subsubtopic: CONFIDENCE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there is not a Canadian today who is not being affected by the serious economic recession in the country. The escalating collapse of our business base, the alarming rise in unemployment, a crippling increase in the cost of consumer goods and services, harshly punitive interest rates, and the indifferent attitude of this government toward its wasteful spending habits have all contributed to the tragic mess we are in today. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby):
That the government use its power, not simply as a means to rule and control arrogantly, but to govern in such a manner that it addresses the real and immediate needs of the people by developing programs with a sense of purpose and direction which will instil confidence in the public and in all sectors of the economy.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REALLOCATION OF FUNDS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the recent news that the Department of Employment and Immigration has earmarked $5 million for an advertising campaign to convince Canadians that the economy as a whole is working, when the reality is that unemployment is at the highest level since 1940, is an insult to the intelligence of Canadians and a slap in the face to those 1.2 million Canadians unemployed as a result of the government's disastrous fiscal and monetary policy. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath):
That, if the government is going to spend the $5 million, it would be better to invest it in job training for the unemployed, instead of wasting it on another attempt by this floundering government to sell itself to the voters with the taxpayers' dollars.

subsubtopic: FUEL COMPENSATION RECOVERY CHARGE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the National Energy Program continues to drive Canadian business south of the border. We have recently learned that British Columbia companies are buying their fuel in the United States at a saving of 30 cents per gallon and that some Great Lakes shippers have called for tenders from the United States. Whereas the National Energy Program's export fuel tax is in part responsible for giving the United States the competitive edge on marine fuel prices, and whereas the government has promised flexibility on this tax, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Erie (Mr. Fretz):
That the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources remove altogether the transportation fuel compensation recovery charge before the United States becomes Canada's number one supplier of marine fuel.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR DISSOLUTION OF PARLIAMENT-MOTION UNDER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Liberal administrations over the past 14 years have consistently promised to fight inflation. It started with the Benson budget in 1968. In 1973 the minister of finance at that time, John Turner, said "This budget is aimed at reducing inflationary pressure in Canada and at offsetting the effect of past inflation." In 1974 the same minister said, "Two digit inflation ... is simply not acceptable to this government." In the same year the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) promised to wrestle inflation to the ground. In 1976 the then finance minister, Donald Macdonald, said "Our first objective must be to maintain the underlying trend to lower inflation." In 1978 the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) said, "We are being held back by serious unemployment and inflation and we must do all we can to deal with them."
It goes on and on. In 1980, 1981 and 1982 the present Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) said the same thing. Madam Speaker, it is obvious that the present administration has lost the battle, inflation has gone from 4 per cent in 1968 to 11.6 per cent today.

That the Prime Minister accept defeat in his battle against inflation, go to the Governor General to dissolve Parliament, call an election immediately, so that Canadians can decide who should be leading the battle against inflation and toward economic renewal.

Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, under the provisions of Standing Order 43.
Yesterday, the provincial court in St. Jerome decided to postpone a ruling on whether or not to evict 77 farmers from expropriated land at Mirabel until May 14. Considering the barbaric action taken by the President of the Canada Lands Company (Mirabel) Ltd., Mr. Jean-Pierre Goyer, to cancel leases and evict farmers who, in fact, were merely trying to buy back land that was expropriated indiscriminately, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy):

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. During the past two years Canadians have been losing their homes, businesses have gone broke in record numbers-a thousand last month alone- and thousands of workers have lost their jobs, all in the name of a high interest rate policy allegedly aimed at curing inflation. Considering that the figures released today show that the cost of living rose more rapidly during the past month than for any period in almost a year, will the government finally admit that it was wrong and abandon this high interest rate dogmatism?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as I have had occasion to explain before to the hon. member, the government does not have a high interest rate policy. There are high interest rates because the rate of inflation is high. Naturally people who save money and put it aside do not want to lend it at low interest rates when the rate of inflation is high. This is why, time after time, I have attempted to convey to the Leader of the New Democratic Party that we do not have a policy of high interest rates, that we have high inflation. The way to bring down interest rates is to bring down inflation. This is why the endless suggestions of the New Democratic Party for spending on this, that, and the next thing, are not helping to bring down inflation. On the contrary, they are helping to increase the deficit, to increase

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Communications, the minister responsible for freedom of information legislation. The minister has refused to appear before the justice committee for over four months, concerning freedom of information legislation, using the excuse that he was waiting for the provincial governments to respond to a uniform act. Now that the majority of the provincial governments have stated that they want nothing to do with a uniform act, when will the minister stop stalling the bill and bring the bill before the justice committee, or will the minister allow the bureaucrats, some of his own cabinet colleagues, and perhaps even the Prime Minister, who has never been particularly enamoured of the idea of freedom of information legislation, to kill this long overdue bill? Specifically, is the minister prepared to give us a commitment that this bill will be brought back before the justice committee in this session of Parliament?

subsubtopic: COMMITTEE STUDY OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, obviously we are all committed to the principle of freedom of information. When the hearings on the bill were suspended in November, it was at the specific request of the attorneys general of just about every province, the sole exception being the province of Manitoba. Since that time a number of the attorneys general who had asked us to pursue the idea of coming up with a uniform bill concerning freedom of information, which indeed would have been a distinct advantage for all advocates of freedom of information, have changed their minds as they feel that the uniform approach would not be productive. However, most of them have maintained a number of objections, as outlined in Mr. McMurtry's letter of November, to the effect that certain of the sections in the actual draft bill which is before the committee ought to be re-examined and changed.
As 1 indicated to the hon. member during the course of my answer to him and to the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton a couple of weeks ago, there were basically three options in front of the government. One was to pursue the uniform bill approach, which is no longer possible since the attorneys
Oral Questions
general have changed their minds. The second was to bring the bill back from the committee without amendment, and the third possibility was, of course, to bring the bill back to the committee with a number of amendments.
I have finished my analysis of the recommendations made to us by the provinces, and I have reported to my cabinet colleagues. This matter is now in front of the cabinet, and once a decision has been taken I will be able to give the hon. gentleman a more forthcoming answer.

subsubtopic: COMMITTEE STUDY OF LEGISLATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, when the minister appeared yesterday before the committee on communications, he did not even indicate that freedom of information legislation was a priority.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the same minister. In view of the fact that the provincial objections centre around two fundamental areas, that is, removal of Crown privilege and the right to independent judicial review, both of which are absolutely critical for an effective freedom of information act, will the minister assure the House that he will in no way water down this fundamental principle of independent judicial review and an end to Crown privilege, both principles which this government, and particularly this Prime Minister, had to be dragged, kicking and screaming, to accept? Can we be assured that these principles will be maintained in any legislation which the government brings back to the justice committee in this session of Parliament?

Madam Speaker, I think there are indeed two questions raised by the hon. member. One concerns the access to information legislation and one concerns Crown privilege. As far as the access to information legislation is concerned, I would very much hope that, as soon as my cabinet colleagues have been able to finish their examination, we will be able to take a definitive position as to when and how we would want to reintroduce the bill or continue hearings in front of the committee.
The hon. member himself has indicated that the main concern of the provincial attorneys general centred around the disappearance of Crown privilege. The hon. member may also know that there have been a couple of court decisions in this country during the course of the fall of 1981 which have changed the common law in many respects concerning Crown privilege. Therefore, it is indeed important to follow the recommendations of the attorneys general, to re-examine the whole question of Crown privilege in the light of evolving jurisprudence in this country and in the countries which follow common law.

Madam Speaker, may I have an undertaking from the Minister of Communications that there will be urgent consideration by the minister

April 21, 1982
Oral Questions
and his colleagues with respect to the matter now that the situation has been changed by the letter of the attorneys general? Will he assure the House that he is considering this to be an urgent matter?
Yes, Madam Speaker, I expect that my cabinet colleagues will be able to consider the matter in due course.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. subsubtopic: FERTILIZER PRICES IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I should like to direct my question to the Minister of Agriculture. Is the minister aware that fertilizer prices in western Canada are between $30 and $60 per tonne higher than they are in the western United States? For the Canadian farmer who is planting a quarter section of land, this means an added cost of roughly $4,000. If he is aware of this situation, can he indicate what action he is planning to overcome what appears to be a grossly unfair situation?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: FERTILIZER PRICES IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am aware of what the hon. member is saying. It is the market system working. There is no tariff on fertilizer moving across the Canada-United States international border. It moves freely. Farmers can go there to purchase fertilizer. I know it would be inconvenient, but I am sure the hon. member does not want me to invoke more regulations concerning control of the sale of fertilizers.
It is said that it is surplus fertilizer being moved into world markets. Approximately 50 per cent of the fertilizer is moved into markets other than the Canadian market. Production is 50 per cent more than is needed for domestic use and is exported. There are three new plants that will come on stream in the next 11 months. That will make those figures look so small it will be amazing. These are nitrogen-producing fertilizer plants that will be producing mostly for the export markets.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, inasmuch as this fertilizer is produced in Canada, will the minister assure the House that he is prepared to meet with the fertilizer companies, or at least prevail upon them to instil some equity and fairness in their marketing practices, particularly in light of the fact that farm input costs are rising dramatically, mainly fuel prices and fertilizer prices, largely as a result of federal government taxes? speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER MEET REPRESENTATIVES OF MANUFACTURING COMPANIES

Madam Speaker, we have a group which meets with the fertilizer manufacturers in Canada. Some of my officials have discussed this informally with them. I addressed this group about three weeks ago in this city. I also pointed out to them in private conversation that we had definite concerns about this fact. It is the market system working in its own fashion. We have deep concern. I repeat, there is no tax on fertilizer coming into or moving out of Canada. There is free trade. It can move freely back and forth across the border. It is an inconvenience. I agree, as the hon. member said, it is unfair that Canadian fertilizer users are being subjected to this.

subtopic: CAPACITY OF WELLAND CANAL TO ACCOMMODATE SHIPPING
CAPACITY OF WELLAND CANAL TO ACCOMMODATE SHIPPING
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. The St. Lawrence Seaway system is in potentially serious trouble if the bottleneck of the Welland Canal is not dealt with very soon. Forecasts of demand for later this decade indicate that up to 65 million tonnes of cargo could be moved through the system, yet the canal's capacity to move this much cargo is fast becoming limited. subtopic: CAPACITY OF WELLAND CANAL TO ACCOMMODATE SHIPPING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the postulate is not right. This is an assessment made by the government of Ontario indicating five years before capacity is reached on the Great Lakes. That study is contradicted by studies made in my department and by the Seaway which estimate it will be a decade before we reach that point. A recent joint study by the Canadian and American Seaway authorities indicated, that 18 or 19 years may be a more accurate estimate. Therefore, there is now plenty of capacity on the Seaway.
Administrative and technological measures of a short-term nature are being taken in order to expand the capacity. Longterm planning for the doubling of the Welland Canal or doing something about the length of the navigation season is also being carried out. Therefore, my friend should not worry too much. Things are well in hand.

Madam Speaker, the minister's answer regarding the task force report by the Ontario government is correct. However, in his report the minister indicated that modernization of the canal, at least some restorative work on the walls of the canal and enlarging the areas in which ships can pass, should be started immediately. What is the minister's answer on that matter?

Madam Speaker, I could send my friend a report on what is now being done by way of administrative and technical changes to the Welland Canal. I will send him that report to assure him that what I said is correct. There will be a number of speeches on this subject in the coming months. There will be a colloquy in the city of Quebec early in June on the Seaway. A lot of good speakers will be there to give reports on the state of navigation on the Seaway and the St. Lawrence.

subsubtopic: MR. HEAP-UNPARLIAMENTARY INTERJECTION DURING MEMBER'S SPEECH
speechtext:

subsubtopic: MR. HEAP-UNPARLIAMENTARY INTERJECTION DURING MEMBER'S SPEECH
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the strictest sense, when a member is charged by the Speaker to withdraw, normally that is the only matter dealt with. That is the issue. When the opposition House leader suggests to you that that is not what the hon. member had said, when in fact he has refused three times to withdraw, then indeed you must instruct him once again to withdraw.
The fact of the matter is, Madam Speaker, that with respect to our rights and privileges the rules apply to everyone on all sides of the House. If the hon. member is going to call someone a liar and he is requested by you to withdraw, he has no alternative but to withdraw.

subsubtopic: MR. HEAP-UNPARLIAMENTARY INTERJECTION DURING MEMBER'S SPEECH
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have been sitting here quietly listening to what has occurred. I listened to what the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) said and, as I recall it, he said, "Madam Speaker, if you wish to substitute the word "fabrication", or "complete fabrication" for "complete lie", that is all right with me". I believe that is a withdrawal.

There is another factor in the matter of using unparliamentary language, which is whether or not it creates a disturbance in the House even if the word is listed. Sometimes it goes by and does not create a disturbance in the House.
I wonder if the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) would feel his honour is restored by the fact that the hon. member for Bow River has substituted "fabrication" for the word he had uttered previously in the House.

subsubtopic: MR. SCHELLENBERGER-SAFETY EQUIPMENT AT LEDUC AREA RAILWAY CROSSINGS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have the duty to present a petition on behalf of my constituents. The purpose of this petition, signed by 1,300 citizens of Leduc and district in the constituency of Wetaskiwin is to urge the government to increase and upgrade the safety equipment at all Leduc area railway crossings. This action is prompted by the occurrences of railway accidents in that area. The petition urges that all railway crossings be equipped with adequate safeguards as rapidly as possible, and that the enforcement of the relevant regulations be rendered more effective.
The petitioners hope you will find the petition in order and will note the great urgency of the circumstances leading up to it, and ask that you use the powers of your office to allow discussion and referral to committee as soon as possible.

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: MR. McGRATH-ESTABLISHMENT OF SEARCH AND RESCUE OPERATIONS IN NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition sponsored by the St. John's Jaycees and signed by 72,000 citizens of Newfoundland. The petition points out the hazardous conditions prevailing in the northwest Atlantic, which was tragically highlighted by the sinking of the oil rig Ocean Ranger with the loss of 82 lives. It points out the dangers to the men who work on these oil rigs, and the men and women who work off the Newfoundland shore in our fisheries and other offshore industries. It also points out the lack of protection our people have at the present time. Your petitioners humbly pray that Parliament directs the government to establish full search and rescue capability in Newfoundland so that its citizens can enjoy the same degree of protection enjoyed by Canadian citizens who work offshore in the maritime provinces.

speechtext:

subsubtopic: $838,100,000. BILINGUAL POSITION IN NEWFOUNDLAND POST OFFICE
speechtext:
1.	Does the government intend to take action with regard to the fact that the 1980 annual report of the Commissioner of Official Languages states there are no bilingual positions in the Post Office Department among Newfoundland's 1,036 postal employees and, if so, what are the details?
2.	For what reason would it be necessary to have bilingual employees in Newfoundland?
3.	What is the estimated percentage of persons living in Newfoundland who speak the (a) English (b) French language only?

speakeroldname: Mr. David Smith (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: $838,100,000. BILINGUAL POSITION IN NEWFOUNDLAND POST OFFICE
speechtext:
I am informed by Canada Post and Statistics Canada as follows:
1.	In Newfoundland, bilingual services are provided, and have been for a number of years, at the Cape St. George Post Office to serve the only area that has an established demand. The Postmaster of this office is employed under the terms of
April 21, 1982

the Post Office Act, therefore is not included in the figures quoted by the Commissioner of Official Languages. As well, Canada Post is committed to the introduction of bilingual services in Labrador City in 1981-82.
2.	As a federal institution, Canada Post recognizes an obligation to provide services in both French and English to Canadians in areas where a demand is established.
3.	The latest information on languages is from the 1976 census, but that information relates only to mother tongue, as opposed to language currently spoken. According to the 1976 census the distribution of the population in Newfoundland by mother tongue was as follows:
Mother tongue English: 97.7 per cent
Mother tongue French: 0.5 per cent
Mother tongue neither English nor French: 1.8 per cent
The most recent information on official languages capabilities was collected in the 1971 census, which asked whether English or French were spoken well enough to conduct a conversation. For Newfoundland, the official languages capabilities of the population in 1971 were:
English only: 98.0 per cent French only: 0.1 per cent Both English and French: 1.8 per cent Neither English nor French: 0.1 per cent
Similar information is being collected in the 1981 census.

The House resumed, from Tuesday, April 20, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill C-105, to amend the Canada Business Corporations Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Energy Legislation.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we adjourned last evening, I was about to analyse the bill, the changes in corporate law, and comment on what this bill can do. This bill affects all corporations in Canada. First, the bill essentially has two major features in it. It allows changes with respect to shareholdings in companies to be handled in two separate ways. For the first time in the history of corporate law this bill will allow a corporation, through its directors, to go into the open market and purchase publicly held shares in the name of the corporation. Those shares will continue to remain outstanding shares of the corporation, albeit not subject to vote and the bill will allow the corporation to qualify under the oil arrangements and under any other provincial or Canadian laws or licence requirements with respect to ownership or control by Canadians.
Let us go into the history of this question of companies being able to trade in their own shares. Corporate law originally set out that a company could not invest in its own shares. A company was prohibited by law from buying up its own shares. In 1974 and 1975 and through that period we changed the corporate law of this country with the Canada Business Corporations Act which allowed a company for the first time to invest in its own shares. The law was changed in order to give a company a great deal more flexibility with respect to financing. Indeed, it allowed a company to use the capital and surplus to buy up shares of shareholders, thus allowing those shareholders to get their investment back and at the same time withdraw their money out of the company. It also allowed for certain takeovers and amalgamations that were possible as a result of a company being allowed to purchase its own shares. But those provisions for purchasing shares only relate to purchasing the shares for cancellation. What a company can do under the present law is to purchase the shares, and when those shares are purchased they are in effect no longer available in the marketplace. They can no longer be put back into the marketplace.
The effect of this bill is to allow a company to purchase its own shares and within a period of two years put those shares back into the marketplace. This is a dramatic change in corporate law which the House must realize is taking place and it is taking place in the name of Canadianization.
The other night I said that patriotism was described as the last refuge of a scoundrel. An appeal to patriotism is the refuge of a scoundrel, which is exactly what this particular provision will allow. For the first time it allows scoundrels to wheel and deal in the corporate stock of their own company. Indeed, it is a very dramatic change to what has been allowed up to now with respect to the activities of companies. I say with all sincerity that this is a very, very serious change in law. What in fact you have is an ability of directors, under the guise of wanting to maintain Canadian ownership and control of their company, to speculate in the stock market with their own stock using the company's own money. When you look at it that way you will say there is something wrong here, Mr. April 21, 1982

Speaker. It may be all very well for us to want to have Canadian ownership of corporations, but in doing that, are we going to allow the possibility of directors of corporations, able to use the company's earned surplus, the company's financial ability, to go into the market and buy up shareholders' shares-they could even be Canadian shareholders' shares because presumably they will be shares purchased on the market-take those shares back in, speculate on them or sell them off privately to some other person? If that is allowed, it is a total misuse of the trusteeship that directors elected for public corporations have to their shareholders. Indeed, the corporations could be private corporations. Therefore, we have a situation for the very first time where a company and the officers of a company can go into the market and use the company's assets to buy shares which the company intends to resell. Indeed, the very purpose of the section is to allow the company to buy the shares to resell.
I have no quarrel with the existing system where a company buys up the shares. If for the purpose of continuing to get credit for Canadian ownership they can buy up the shares to qualify in some way for ownership and control in terms of the crazy rules and regulations that were proposed under Bill C-104, that is all right, but what we have here is a situation where the corporation, through its directors, is allowed to speculate using shareholders' equity, to speculate and play around with the shareholders' own money, for private benefit. This is a dramatic change in what until now has been the basis of sound corporate practice. When we make changes in the way corporate law is structured, we not only seriously affect the value of corporate stocks of companies affected by the possible change, but we generally hurt or damage the reputation of federally-incorporated companies. This is a serious concern which the House must address.
Another change in the act involves a provision which was originally contained in Bill C-94. Significant changes have been made to Bill C-94 as a result of the efforts of my party in drawing to public attention the damages inherent in it. Those changes resulted in other portions of the constrained share regulations being altered as they were in the first paragraph on the top of page 9 of the bill. Nonetheless, as pointed out by the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens), the changes to Section 43 of the Canada Business Corporations Act that were followed up with amendments to Sections 122 and 168 of the act do not seem to have solved the problem totally.
The essence of Section 43.1 in Part V.l on page 4 of Bill C-105 is that a company should be entitled, in order to keep its qualification in line, to expropriate somehow the shares of shareholders, then sell those shares to other persons and pay the expropriated shareholders the net value of or the net receipt from the sale. It is true that this only applies where there are constrained shares, but I submit that the definition of constrained shares in inadequate. The details as to how the expropriation sale and eventual distribution of net proceeds are to be effected are not properly set out. Indeed, the entire
Canada Business Corporations Act
concept that directors of a company should somehow be entitled to seize a shareholder's share for which the shareholder has paid, to sell it in the marketplace as if the shareholder never owned it and to pay the net proceeds to the person selected to be expropriated, must be offensive to us all. It is not a fair compensation for property or even an ordinary expropriation. It is an actual seizure and payment of net proceeds to the holder of the share. In other words, all the costs of the expropriation are borne by the person expropriated.
Let me turn to a situation wherein one's property is taken over by the Ontario department of highways. Departmental officials could say that they had to appraise it, do this or that, and that they had only been able to obtain so much for the property, and turn over the net proceeds. This is what we are talking about. While the provision refers to constrained shares, there is no provision with respect to what the constrained shareholder will in fact receive. There is provision in the bill for notice to the constrained shareholder that he had better sell his share or shares, but if there is little or no market, but only hopes for opportunities with those shares, then he could be virtually expropriated without any compensation because in fact he is forced to sell and all he receives as a result of the sale are the net proceeds. In a weak market such as the one of today he could be wiped out. Both of these provisions are bad ones and should not be included in the statute law.
It is one thing to talk about Canadian ownership. I think we want Canadian ownership. But to include these provisions in the Canada Business Corporations Act is wrong. It is wrong to allow directors of a corporation-or the majority of shareholders of a corporation organizing with the directors-to so damage the interest of other shareholders, for the alleged purpose of Canadianizing or allowing the corporation to take advantage of some provincial privilege or some other privilege in some other statute. The hon. member for York-Peel produced in the House a series of Ontario and federal statutes which particularly require some element or a totality of Canadian ownership and control. It is also wrong to allow minority shareholders, albeit foreign or perhaps not that foreign, to be expropriated without really being compensated or to allow, as in the first part of the bill, directors to go into the marketplace to wheel and deal with the money of shareholders, to favour some persons over other persons. These provisions are wrong.
There is no need for this bill. Even if we were to go along with the government's Canadian ownership package with respect to grants to the oil industry, we do not need this bill. Companies can change their incorporations. They can create more shares. They can request supplementary articles of association to give them larger capital. They can organize their control in many other fashions. They do not need these powers. Inasmuch as these powers extend beyond the oil and energy industry, they should not be in this piece of legislation because they do not properly belong there. Therefore, I suggest that we must oppose this bill.

Canada Business Corporations Act
I would like to review for a moment some events which are occurring in the marketplace. Yesterday and today articles appeared in The Globe and Mail which contained parts of a speech given by Mr. W. A. Macdonald to an IBM conference in Banff, Alberta. Mr. Macdonald is from the law firm of McMillan, Binch, and you realize there is another famous partner of that firm who used to be in the House. Apparently, Mr. Macdonald and that former member got along well and I suspect they compared notes with respect to this presentation.
In any event, in Mr. Macdonald's speech he listed some elements of Canadian financial policy which were important to the Canadian nation. In that speech, which appeared in The Globe and Mail on April 20, he said:
Canada has an open economy, which is deeply dependent on world trade in goods and services and on international capital flows. This has always required a recognition that there are severe restraints on insular policy-making, based on a false premise as to the ability of any Canadian government to control the details of the Canadian economy against the power of external economic forces.
He said further:
Canada has an isolated economy with a small market alongside the largest and most powerful economy in the world. Canada has always sought to handle these special vulnerabilities by a twofold approach: first, to support a stable, relatively free, multilateral and financial order; second, to develop a close, but not too close, relationship with the United States, whereby trading and financial particulars can be worked out within the framework of a stable, multilateral order and on the basis of constructive, mutual self-interest.
In other words, until now our success was based on those rules which provide a stable arrangement in our corporate law and state that we do not attempt to be too ultra-nationalistic and that we rely on the financial power of the New York marketplace to a great extent.
Speaking to that very issue, Mr. Macdonald said in the same article:
... Canada continues to increase its foreign debt at an accelerating rate. Much of this foreign debt is long term and floated in the New York market. The limited funds available in relation to expected demand in that market have resulted in high interest rates.
He went on to say:
Can we really believe we can increase our claims on the New York financial market and persist in our unwillingness to acknowledge any U.S. concerns as to major unfairness and protectionist elements in the NEP and FIRA? Is it realistic to believe we can continue to enjoy unimpeded access to U.S. financial markets while the overcrowding of U.S. government issues arising out of their rapidly growing deficit is already threatening both the economic recovery in the United States and the entire economic revolution on which President Reagan is staking his political future?
He says further:
At the very time when the country needs to put its strongest economic foot forward to offset the costs of the present world economic situation, we have been pursuing increasingly interventionist, nationalist and provincialist policies.
That is what this legislation is, a policy which is part of an attempt somehow to Canadianize not only the oil industry but other industries as well. This is to be accomplished by changing the very fabric of the Canada Business Corporations Act to allow individuals-not the government-to expropriate shares and pay not the market price but the net proceeds for those shares. It will allow directors of Canadian corporations to use shareholders' money in the marketplace, to expel foreign
shareholders and perhaps to favour their own friends and others.
There are provisions in the bill for rules and regulations to be proclaimed by the government. But the problem with imposing regulations in corporate law by order in council is that laws of this nature can be changed at will. In other words, there can be regulations which will protect the investor to make sure that directors do not, at their discretion, play with the stock market.
To have rules imposed in this manner is not the answer because there is no certainty as to what future regulations will be. Instead, rules with respect to financial transactions of this nature and to the activities of corporations should be clearly stipulated in a statute. In this way, regulations could only be changed by an act of Parliament through the usual process of three readings here and in the other place and through committee hearings.
The difficulty arising from regulations which are made by order in council is that no committee hearings are required. We would only find out about a regulation after it has been made. Changes can be made again and again without any opportunity to prevent the government from changing the rules in the middle of the game. Protection for minority shareholders is not set out in the statute in any detail. The details required with respect to stipulations for directors of companies buying shares and then reselling them are not set out in the bill. For example, directors could buy for $10 and sell for $20 or perhaps even sell for $5 to friends and thus rape the treasury of the company.
There is no requirement that they can only buy from foreign shareholders. It only stipulates that in order to keep Canadian ownership content they must buy shares in the market. Do they buy Canadian shares or what? When shares are purchased on the stockmarket there is no way of knowing whether they are foreign or Canadian shares. Indeed, with the manner in which shares are handled presently, behind trusts and pension plans and in street form, it is difficult to know who owns what.
You could be buying Canadian shares but you would not really know. It is true that the intent is to buy foreign-held shares in Canadian corporations, but these shares are purchased through the use of shareholders' money, and that is what I believe is wrong. I see nothing wrong with a company investing in its own shares provided those shares are then cancelled. Companies would then buy the shares in the marketplace and reduce the number of shares outstanding. However, that is not the case here. I see nothing wrong with the situation where a share was specifically issued which could only be held by a Canadian-a living Canadian individual and not a Canadian corporation-and a share was not a share unless it was in fact registered to a living Canadian. If that living Canadian sold his share to a foreigner, then that living Canadian would lose his rights in that share. That would be possible. I see nothing wrong with that. However, that is not
April 21, 1982

what is in this bill. This bill speaks of constrained shares and then it says that a constraint must be shown on the face of the constrained shares, but it does not say there is anything wrong with shares which do not have any notification of constraint on them. There is a provision in the bill for shares which are not dealt with as constrained shares because when they were originally issued they were not then constrained shares.
Therefore, this a bad law. It is important that the bill go to committee, but it is even more important that members of Parliament who are concerned about the kind of laws we have realize that this bill contains bad law. I see that the minister responsible for foreign affairs is here in the House. As he is a former law professor, I think he should be concerned about the bad law in this bill. This bill should be considered and it should be withdrawn. I say it has nothing to do with the Canadian ownership concept of the oil industry. The bill goes beyond that. It affects all corporations. It affects our activities, fund raising and financial arrangements whereby Canadian companies, in some cases, are listed on the New York market, and properly so. A number of our major companies are there. They use the New York market, which is really the world finance market. Certainly, we use either the London or New York market to raise funds. Much of those funds must be raised by shares issue or share pledge. Consequently, a company needs to have its shares listed in those markets. It is not good for Canada to be so insular as to make it possible that changes could be made which would affect those shares now being issued in other countries when there is a cutback in the trading position of companies largely held in Canada, indeed, with the majority of the shareholders presently in Canada.
Therefore, I say that this bill is a bad bill. It should be defeated. It must be defeated.

Mr. Speaker, I wanted to speak briefly on Bill C-105. Let me first say that in my estimation this is a dangerous bill. This is a new dimension in corporate practice, and I do not like it.
The government is overly obsessed with Canadianization of the oil and gas industry in Canada. By 1990 it wants the industry to be 50 per cent Canadian owned. The time-frame is too short. The methods of the government, like this Bill C-105, are devious and destructive to government and industry relationships and particularly to federal-provincial relationships. The economic climate generated on the short term is one in which there is a flight of capital, a flight of technological competence and a flight of management skills.
In 1977, as the newspaper reported today, there was a Canadian capital outflow of some $265 million. By 1980, the outward flow was $2.2 billion. In 1981, it increased to $10.2 billion. The cause of this terrific increase has been stated to be the National Energy Program and subsequent legislation. How can our economy, which is geared to megaprojects, possibly recover? We desperately need capital, yet the government
Canada Business Corporations Act
works furiously to drive capital away. How does it intend to bring capital into the nation to build the vast megaprojects that we have before us? This must surely be some form of selfstrangulation.
Yesterday the minister told us that last year the investment in the energy industry dropped by some 30 per cent to 40 per cent. I think he acknowledged that. Yesterday he also advised the House that the U.S. department of commerce, in its recent report, projected an increase of investment of 28 per cent in the energy sector in Canada this year. However, the minister did not tell us how much investment on Canada lands was projected as against the protection for provincial lands. He did not tell us whether this projection included investment in Alsands or projects like it.
I can understand, and even to a partial degree accept without too much difficulty, the Canadianization program worked out in Bill C-48 concerning Canada lands. This is a future course dictated by political philosophy and perspective. All companies know the rules in advance so that the private sector will behave accordingly and form the necessary partnerships and consortiums to explore, develop and market, knowing full well that no less than 25 per cent will be under Canadian ownership and that, in most cases, it will be more. This is very similar to the Norwegian policies which were explained to us in detail when we were debating Bill C-48. There is nothing wrong with that type of approach, whether one agrees with Canadianization or not. It is a future movement. The new regimes of state ownership and Canadianization can readily be imposed on the new development, in new areas, under the jurisdiction of a single regime under Canada lands.
Canadianization on Canadian lands is done under a single regime: the federal government. It does not involve the provincial governments. However, to try to impose a devious regime of Canadianization on an entire industry, presently almost entirely limited to activity on provincial lands, exploiting provincial resources, is no less than economic madness. The federal government can administer PIP, as it has indicated, on federal lands to Canadianize, if it wishes. Surely, this is appropriate action, but it should surely allow the provinces to administer PIP on provincial lands in accordance with provincial policies, provincial priorities and provincial political perspectives which may not be associated with the rapid Canadianization. Why not? Why must the federal government dictate to the provinces that it shall Canadianize their industry on their own resources at a certain rate so that they will be 50 per cent Canadianized by 1990? Why must the government insist on this in order for those companies working in the provinces, on provincial resources, to receive the PIP grants? I find this difficult to accept. As a result, the whole Canadianization program is badly curtailing the oil and gas sector on provincial lands, particularly Alberta. I say again that I have no difficulty if that is what the federal government wants to do with Canada lands. It is a single jurisdiction dictating the development of a massive new industry where they are fully responsible.

April 21, 1982
Canada Business Corporations Act
Today we have two governments fighting over maximizing their economic take. One is bent on getting due economic rent for its resources. The other, the federal government, is massively bleeding the industry through the PGR tax and incremental taxes. It is partially using such taxes as incentives through the PIP program to force corporate reorganization, corporate refinancing and corporate restructuring of companies developing provincial resources.
The federal government through this legislation is poaching upon provincial areas of jurisdiction. In my estimation, it is severely undermining the very intent of Sections 50 and 51 of the Constitution just patriated. That section is very explicit. It reads:
In each province, the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to
(a)	exploration for non-renewable natural resources in the province;
(b)	development, conservation and management of non-renewable natural resources and forestry resources in the province, including laws in relation to the rate of primary production therefrom; and
(c)	development, conservation and management of sites and facilities in the province for the generation and production of electrical energy. ...
(4) In each province, the legislature may make laws in relation to the raising of money by any mode or system of taxation in respect of
(a)	non-renewable natural resources and forestry resources in the province and the primary production therefrom, and
(b)	sites and facilities in the province for the generation of electrical energy and the production therefrom,
How can a province maximize its take from its own resource and have freedom in relation to taxation when the federal government comes in in a massive way with a big hand and takes a major portion at the front end? This taxation is only possible after the federal government gets its take. If there is nothing left, the provincial government gets nothing. This section in the Constitution tends to be meaningless. The federal government can make it meaningless. I find that contradictory to the very intent of this section and in fact contrary to the patriated Constitution.
The federal government is trying to impose its political philosophy on the provinces in the development of provincially-owned resources. That is wrong. It is unconstitutional in accordance with the new Constitution. Surely Saskatchewan can nationalize all it wishes and Alberta can promote free enterprise regardless of ownership all it wishes in the development of resources without the hand of Big Brother in Ottawa forcing its political philosophy and direction on the provinces.
This is basic to the patriated Constitution. It is very basic to Sections 50 and 51 of it. I find that a very serious anomaly in this area. The constitutionality of this legislation must be tested in the courts at the earliest possible time.
I repeat, I have no dificulty with the federal government Canadianizing the industry on federal lands. It is a single jurisdiction. It has every right to do that and to do it as it wishes. However, when it involves itself in Canadianization of provincial lands, it must respect provincial authority and the provincial constitutional rights which those provinces have in connection with their resources.
I can understand the desire of the national government and its philosophy in imposing the Canadianizing requirement on industries involved in renewable resources and industries involved in non-renewable resources such as oil and gas where it has sole jurisdiction, like Canada lands. With renewable resources such as electricity, governments all across the nation, with the exception of Alberta, have got involved because that goes on forever.
To force that on the provinces with regard to provincial nonrenewable resources is unacceptable, particularly when some of them have a lifetime of only five or ten years. Why would a government want to Canadianize companies having a resource if it wants to do additional exploration and it only has a five to ten-year lifetime on that resource? Surely it would want to Canadianize a renewable resource industry such as fisheries, forestry, hydroelectricity, but why Canadianize something with a very finite lifetime? I find it difficult to understand. The only explanation I can give is that it has not been fully thought out. It must be examined more fully.
Why would a government or any political philosophy generate such economic instability to Canadianize an industry involved in non-renewable resources which have a very finite lifetime? If the government wants money, surely it can tax the industry to its heart's desire. If it wants to control and discourage capital outflow, it can tax dividends as heavily as it wishes and make them non-tax deductible.
A government with restrictive conditions imposed on the Canadian subsidiaries of multinational companies will have these overseas branches stripped from them at the earliest opportunity. Instead of having Canadian companies with a multinational effect throughout the world, we will have Canadian companies with little association with world industry, with a limit in terms of technological interchange and exchange.
Multinational oil and gas subsidiary corporations in Canada are good citizens. They employ only Canadians. They reinvest most of their generated cash flow in Canada. Many do massive research in Canada such as the Syncrude project, Suncor and the heavy oil Cold Lake plants. The world knows that in Alberta and Canada we are at the forefront of technological development in heavy oils, oilsands and in many other areas, in drilling, for example. The world runs to Alberta to get our technology, so no one can say research is being done outside the country in this particular industry. It is done in Canada. We are the experts in this area. If the South Americans want heavy oils, they come to Alberta to get the technology. One cannot say we must Canadianize if we want research to be done here.
I can understand policies which limit the corporate size of Canadian subsidiaries of multinationals to prevent massive accumulation and concentration of assets because a diversity of small companies is always healthier than just a few major ones in a particular industry. I can understand a government, whether it is provincial or federal, withholding licences and
April 21, 1982

permits from foreign-owned corporations. I can also understand-but I reject-the myriad government controls and regulations imposed on the oil and gas industry, although much too often they are excessive and expensive. If governments control, regulate, monitor, tax heavily and restrict corporate growth, what earthly reason is there for Canadiani-zation, or even nationalization, of a corporate entity producing non-renewable resources which have a finite lifetime? We can do anything we wish with the companies or industry now. We can destroy them overnight, as is being done in western Canada. What earthly reason is there for trying to Canadian-ize something which has a very finite lifetime? I find it difficult to understand the reasoning. It is only because a few politicians hunger and thirst for power without ever really having earned the right to it or knowing what the industry is all about. There is a massive design and desire to control what belongs to the people in any event. The resources belong entirely to the people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are continuing with this marathon that we started the week before Easter. We are not beginning debate on the seventh bill dealing with energy. The bill we have before us this afternoon consists of amendments to the Petroleum Administration Act. The act will be renamed the Energy Administration Act and formal authority is being sought for several oil and gas pricing and compensation initiatives.
First, this bill will establish a new ceiling of $75 per cubic metre for the petroleum compensation charge on refiners and importers and broaden the scope for payment of compensation to include new domestic oil.
Second, it will establish a new oil export charge ceiling of $350 per cubic metre and provide us with authority to share one-half of the revenue from this charge with the producing provinces.
Third, it will establish the Canadian ownership special charge and the Canadian ownership account and ensure the charge cannot be raised above its current level without additional legislation.
Fourth, it will establish the transportation fuel compensation recovery charge on marine and aviation fuel used by carriers in international transportation with a ceiling of $350 per cubic metre. It will establish authority for and terminate the special compensation charge which had been established at the time of the breakdown in our negotiations with the Government of Alberta.
April 21, 1982



The basic elements of this legislation, Mr. Speaker, are directly related to the main goals of the National Energy Program. They include expanding the application of the petroleum compensation charge, which will enhance the effectiveness of higher prices for new oil as an incentive to undertake exploration and development operations. This promises to strengthen the energy security of Canadians and promote industrial activity in western Canada. The increasing importance of Petro-Canada is another vital element of the energy program that has been incorporated in this bill. Previously, a major step was made in this direction when the Crown corporation acquired Petrofina Canada, while the Canadian ownership special charge covers the major part of the cost of this acquisition. One of the main goals of the National Energy Program is to end our dependence on foreign oil by 1990. We shall honour this commitment, while maintaining a fair and realistic pricing system that will be acceptable to both the oil industry and the general public.
Our oil and gas pricing schedule, as created in consultation with the provinces, reflects the sense of realism and fairness which characterizes our energy program. Our pricing system has three essential advantages over the regime proposed by the previous Conservative government in 1980. It ensures that prices rise gradually and predictably so that consumers and the Canadian economy in general are given time to adjust. It ensures oil pricing fairness on a national level by providing a blended price to all regions of the country, and it results in a consumer price which has been and will continue to be lower than that paid by people of most other countries.
The Conservative government proposed in 1979 to pay one price to producers of oil in Canada except synthetic oil, regardless of the cost of developing and producing different types of oil. Moreover, the price was directly linked to 85 per cent of the international price, whatever the international price might be, thereby directly exposing Canadian consumers to the uncertainties of international oil prices regardless of the consequences to the country's economy.

This kind of pricing system would have forced Canadian consumers to spend several billion dollars more on already discovered oil and old oil, and to keep paying higher prices although at the time the oil was discovered, production costs were much lower. In addition, under the same system, production of new oil in Canada would not have been as profitable as it is elsewhere. I think people will find that our pricing system is entirely different and more sensible.

Our pricing system provides producers with the kind of return on investments they need to get on with the job of finding and producing oil for Canada-no more, no less.
Energy Administration Act
Returns on existing oil production have not been increased appreciably. However, returns from our new oil reference price created by the energy agreement with Alberta compare favourably with returns offered anywhere else in the world. This price applies to all companies developing new oil anywhere in Canada. This regime provides the Canadian economy with the certainty and stability needed to plan sound economic development in the 1980s.
At the wellhead prices for old oil, that is oil discovered before December 1980, will rise gradually and predictably at a fixed schedule to no more than 75 per cent of the international price. Unlike Conservative budget proposals, this price is not fully linked to the world price. It reflects the fact that this oil was relatively easy and certainly less expensive to develop than oil discovered recently. The substantially higher new oil reference price will be paid to producers of oil discovered after December 31, 1980, to producers of synthetic oil and new frontier production.
This reference price will provide a powerful incentive to producers to develop new oil supplies. It will never exceed world prices. Also, in the event that world prices rise sharply, the new oil price has a provision for phasing in increases, thereby protecting Canadian consumers.

Prices for recently discovered conventional oil, imported oil, frontier oil and synthetic oil are weighted in order to set a price that will apply in all areas of Canada. Today, the weighted price, that is, the average blended price for all oil produced in Canada and imported oil is 70 per cent of the world oil price. Oil that may be sold at the new reference price, plus imported oil, account for 36 per cent of the weighted price. Although this percentage may increase during the period covered by the energy agreement concluded with Alberta, we expect that the lower price for conventional oil will still constitute the major part of the weighted price when the agreement expires in 1986, thus keeping the weighted price below world levels. Our blended price, or average price if you prefer, which will apply to all imported or Canadian oil, will guarantee not only that Canadians will pay much lower prices than consumers in other countries, but also much lower prices than they would have had to pay with the Progressive Conservative budget.

The opposition continually attacks our pricing system on the basis of gasoline prices at the pumps. Its spokesmen never bother to point out to the general public that the Government of Canada does not control retail gasoline prices. We establish the price refiners pay for the crude they buy. This is the blended price. As I indicated, it stood at about 70 per cent of the world price in January of this year. If we included only the price of the old oil or oil discovered in Canada and exploited before December 31, 1980, we would have a price for old oil which is 54 per cent of the international price.

April 21, 1982
Energy Administration Act
The integrated or blended price for all oil produced in Canada stands at the present time at about 70 per cent of the world price. After refiners purchase their crude at the blended price several costs, many of which are not under our control, are added to the price. For instance, they include the cost of refining and transporting oil to markets. They include profit margins for refiners and retailers and, very significantly, they include retail sales taxes. These retail sales taxes in turn include a constant 9 per cent in federal taxes, and then from zero to 40 per cent in provincial taxes depending upon the province-zero per cent in Alberta, 40 per cent in Quebec, and various levels of taxation according to the provinces.

Obviously Mr. Speaker, Canadians are in a good position because our blended price is still only 70 per cent of world prices and will remain much lower over the next four years. It is interesting to note the substantial at-the-pump tax in some provinces, including those provinces which pretend to be concerned about the impact of rising energy costs on their economy. In this regard, I would once again point out that Quebec has the highest sales tax in Canada, namely a 40 per cent sales tax on gasoline at the pump and this tax means gasoline prices in Quebec are the highest in Canada.

But even with substantial provincial taxes, the price of gas at the pumps continues to be half what it is in most European countries. It is rather difficult to compare Canadian and American prices because of differing sales taxes in the two countries and varying prices throughout the United States. I would invite my hon. friends to have a little patience. I will answer all their arguments, including those questions they will ask in the next few days.
I would like to deal with the comparison between Canada and the United States and explain it quite clearly on the record. I would point out that before sales taxes-I have talked about those sales taxes before-gasoline in the United States cost 36 cents a litre while in Canada at the present time it is only 29 cents a litre. That is a difference of 7 cents. However, it is clear that this substantial price advantage offered to consumers by our blanket pricing system is eliminated in many provinces through retail sales taxes imposed by provincial governments. I have indicated that provincial sales taxes vary in this country from zero cents in Alberta to 13 cents per litre in Quebec. The highest sales tax in any state in the United States goes up to 4.5 cents a litre, about three times less than the highest tax in a province in Canada. In effect, this means that you have a significant difference at the pump due to large differences between provincial taxes in Canada and state taxes in the United States.
Obviously, I do not challenge the right of provincial governments to impose such taxes. But I want to make it clear to the Canadian public that it is the provinces, not the Government of Canada, that are taking away the benefits offered by our blended pricing system in those provinces where they have very high sales taxes indeed.
The petroleum compensation charge is an integral part of the blended pricing system. It is the charge that will be used to ensure that the producers of new oil receive the new oil reference price for their production. This ensures that producers receive a fair price for their oil.
The petroleum compensation charge also ensures fairness among regions in Canada. As we know, certain parts of Quebec and all of Atlantic Canada depend upon high cost imported oil to meet a substantial portion of their energy needs. The Government of Canada has taken steps to ensure that these regions will soon have access to domestic oil and gas production but these efforts will take a few years to come to fruition. Since 1974, it has been the policy of the Government of Canada that no region in Canada should have to pay substantially higher oil costs because an accident of history and geography has made them dependent upon imported oil.
Currently, the largest portion of the petroleum compensation charge is used to compensate refiners in these regions for the difference in the international oil price they must pay and the price paid by refiners in other parts of the country who have access to less expensive domestic production.

Mr. Speaker, Canada has benefited greatly from the petroleum compensation charge which, since its introduction by our government in 1974, has cushioned the Canadian economy and Canadian consumers against the shock caused by the sudden major increases of world oil prices throughout the seventies. Since 1974, this charge has been used to pay $13.7 billion in compensation to those regions of Canada, namely Quebec and the Atlantic provinces, which, because of their geographic location and their history, have had to rely in varying degrees on imported oil to meet their energy requirements. This is what our government means by equity and this is what we have really done for consumers in this country, especially those in eastern Canada who were in a very unfavourable position. These moneys have been spent to ensure that Canadians across the country will pay similar prices for the oil they need.

This bill contains a major provision relating to an important goal of the National Energy Program, that of vastly expanding the opportunities for Canadians in the petroleum industry.
We are seeking formal authority for the Canadian ownership special charge which provides the means to allow the Government of Canada to expand its ownership in the oil and gas industry. Revenue from the charge which is placed in the Canadian ownership account is currently being used to help defray the cost of Petro-Canada's purchase of Petrofina slightly more than a year ago. In future, revenue could be used to finance additional purchases on behalf of Petro-Canada, the government or other Crown corporations created for the purpose of expanding public sector involvement in the oil industry. But I want to make it clear that no future acquisitions will be financed from this account without Parliament
April 21, 1982

having the choice to debate the matter through the negative resolution procedure.
It is clear that the Canadian people support an aggressive public sector presence to promote projects that will make a major contribution to energy security and encourage the Canadian private sector to get involved.
Some commentators in the House, and outside, have complained about these charges in aggregate. It is not so much that they quarrel with the purchase of each charge, but they say that the cumulative effect on consumers is excessive. A fair-minded observer, however, would recognize that Canadians support these measures as an investment in securing our own energy future. Each charge in this bill serves a specific purpose related to one of the golas of the National Energy Program. They are the means whereby the government can carry out the major goals of the National Energy Program for the benefit of all Canadians.
In that respect I was interested to read today the most recent report by the Canadian Petroleum Association on the proven reserves, especially after having heard all the moans from the Conservative benches during the last few weeks. It is interesting that this report that was made by the Canadian Petroleum Association-not by the government-indicated that in 1981, the year about which our friends on the other side complained so much, we have had an increase in established oil reserves in Canada for the first time in many years. An increase, Mr. Speaker, when our established reserves had been decreasing each previous year.
In 1981 a very significant increase was also obtained in our established reserves in oil and gas. This happened after the National Energy Program had been proclaimed and started to come into effect.
I would also stress that some of the charges indicated here contain an increase in the maximum that is set for those charges. This does not mean that the government is increasing those charges to that level. This provides a ceiling under which the charges can be varied according to the needs. For instance, each month the National Energy Board reviews the petroleum compensation charge and my department reviews how much we need to pay the refiners for imported petroleum. When the petroleum which is imported decreases in price, the charge decreases. If the price of imported petroleum increases, the charge obviously has to increase to pay the difference between the Canadian price and the imported price.
This is the reason we need to have that flexibility, to enable us to vary the charge every month, for instance. Similarly, this applies to the export charge on oil that we export to the United States. We need the flexibility to vary this charge. This is the reason this bill provides for possible increases in the level of those charges.
This bill represents a very fundamental part of our National Energy Program and I commend it to the House. I urge all hon. members to give their strong support to the bill.
Energy Administration Act

There seems to be some pent-up need on the part of others to participate, and I welcome their participation. He would be less critical if he was aware of the issues. However, if he feels a need to speak, I certainly hope he takes advantage of the opportunity the House of Commons provides. If he feels his speech would contribute to a reduction in the feelings of frustration, anger and rage which cause people in the hundreds and thousands in western Canada to look at separatism as an answer, and if he can allay their concerns and cause those meetings to decrease in number, then I would welcome that speech. I sincerely would, but I am afraid that is not likely to occur.
So far the only answer from the government is an advertising campaign which brings more people out to such meetings. They know why they are angry, and when they see ads on television with geese flying into the sunset and the government saying "We have to inform you", the implication is: "Look, you dummies out there, you don't know what is going on. If you watch these ads, they will make you know what is going on, and then you won't want to join the WCC." The $70 million the government is spending on advertising is not just money down the drain; it is contributing to the membership of the WCC, but the government does not seem to understand.
There were marvellous promises made. There was no way the party opposite would allow an 18 cents tax increase. Hon. members opposite said: "Vote Liberal and we will keep the price of gasoline down". Vote Liberal and pay more than $2 a gallon for gasoline. We pay $1.35 in taxes alone. We have to listen to the minister say he is keeping our prices below the world level. What do we have to do to get a minister to tell us
the truth? Can we expect truth out of our national government?

Canadian airline and oil industry officials are shaking their heads in disbelief at a complex new fuel tax system now being proposed by the federal government.
A direct tax on aviation fuel used for international flights has been withdrawn following complaints by other countries that the tax violated bilateral air agreements.
What we are asked to approve in Bill C-103 is a tax the government cannot impose because it violates International Air Transport Association agreements. However, the government has collected it, so we now have to pass a law to legalize a tax collected previously which the government was not allowed to collect. Can hon. members believe that? And the government says "Vote for us and we will keep prices down"!
Let me quote from this article again:
"I think they (federal officials) are out of their minds," said Gordon Lindsay of the Air Transport Association of Canada.
"This is the most complex thing I've ever seen pulled on a tax."
The article goes on with equally complimentary comments about the competence of this government, to which those-to use the description of the Prime Minister-"trained donkeys" say, "Aye, sir, aye, we approve; we think you are wonderful and doing just a great job."

Then the petroleum compensation charge is a dandy. That was brought in originally to set up a special fund to subsidize Syncrude production to domestic levels. We passed an act in this House, with relative dispatch, which provided that there shall be collected on every barrel of oil in Canada sufficient funds to subsidize the Syncrude price down to world levels, or production from any other tar sands plants which might come along. It was somewhat like unemployment insurance. It was a special fund. It did not go into consolidated revenue. It was not a tax. It was not preceded by a Ways and Means motion, which would have been required if it was a tax. It was a special fund to take care of the Syncrude situation, which arose out of an agreement between various provinces and others which participated. The government decided to raise more money to subsidize imports. It was not getting enough from the export tax. An excise tax could have done it, but in the election campaign the Liberal Party made a big thing about excise taxes, so it could not use excise taxes. The government had to invent a new tax. It has the same effect. It still hurts when you pay it out of your jeans when you buy gasoline, but the government would not use the horrible words "excise tax." It was the petroleum compensation charge. One of the geniuses-one of the "Tanzanianizers"-in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources discovered that perhaps the government could use this petroleum compensation charge. Lo and behold, on July 10, 1980, the minister comes tramping in and lays down a piece of paper, saying: "This is a notice of ways and means; effective midnight tonight you will now pay more for the petroleum compensation charge".
I raised a point of order and asked: "How can you do that? How can you just lay down a piece of paper and suddenly start collecting money, since the bill you purport to amend by that ways and means motion was not a tax bill in the first instance but a special fund?" Madam Speaker said: "That is a legal problem; I cannot deal with it, sorry."
We then sought legal counsel and were told: "You are right, it is illegal; they are not supposed to do that". We asked: "How much would it cost to pursue this?" The reply was: "About $200,000." We just do not happen to have $200,000 to spare in order to require the government to keep the law. That is all we are asking-that the government obey the law.
Finally, in Bill C-103 the government is trying to catch up and make legal what is illegal. This time it introduced a notice of Ways and Means, and so suddenly something that was not a tax is defined as a tax. How that magic transformation occurred I have no idea. I asked legal counsel for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, Mr. Elwood, how that could be. He replied; "Just because there is a procedural imperfection, that does not mean it is not a tax." Just because there is a procedural imperfection? It is as if he were saying: "Look, you turkey, you Member of Parliament, you are just a sausage factory. You are supposed to spit out whatever we geniuses decide. You should not be asking us to obey all of these little procedural niceties in the House of Commons." That is simply

unbelievable, Mr. Speaker. And we are supposed to live in a parliamentary democracy!
I recommend that members examine a letter I received from the Standing Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments which is signed by the two chairmen, Senator John Godfrey, a Liberal, and the Hon. Perrin Beatty, a Conservative. It states that the government is currently breaking the law in regard to the export tax, that it is collecting more than it is authorized to collect by law. What do you do with a government that refuses to obey the law, Mr. Speaker? Some people feel that you must go to Western Canada Concept meetings. Unfortunately, that is what they feel. Is that not sad?
This business about the petroleum compensation charge has not stopped yet. The government collects the equivalent of 24 cents per gallon now, or about $3 billion per year. Now it wants us to give it authority to allow that to be raised to $7.5 billion per year without having to ask the House for permission.

Well, on this one they were asking for authority to raise 70 cents per gallon. The minister says: "Ah, but this is just to subsidize imports and will not be abused." I would remind him of what one of his predecessors, Mr. Macdonald, said about the export tax. He said that it would be used for import subsidization. But not any more, Mr. Speaker; it is for another purpose. I would remind him of what the Hon. John Turner said about the excise tax on gasoline. In his budget of 1975 he said that it would be used for import subsidization. Where is it going now? It is going into other revenues.
The minister stands up and says: "Don't worry about that 48 cents per gallon, about that $7.5 billion. We won't abuse it; we will just use it for import subsidization." To that I say: "Listen, when two of your predecessors gave us a line like that and then had it flipped around, why in blazes would we believe you now?"-unless, of course, one was a trained donkey.
It is absurd that we are asked to give the government authority to collect that kind of tax without ever having to come back to this House. It is an incredible principle that we should be asked to turn over to the Crown the authority to raise taxes at will without ever getting the approval of Parliament. That bears no resemblance to parliamentary democracy; it bears a closer resemblance to a dictatorship.
Related to that and just as offensive is this Canadian ownershipcharge. That is a sneaky little deal, another sneaky little tax which amounts to four cents per gallon or $800 million per year. It is being used to pay off the purchase of
